02/08/2026, 11:04 pm - PARIL: Myth 5: Intelligence Tests Are Biased Against Certain Groups of People.

The claim that modern intelligence tests are broadly biased against certain racial or ethnic groups is largely a psychological myth, as professional psychometric evaluations demonstrate equal predictive validity across major demographic groups. However, confusion persists because group score differences are often misconstrued as technical test bias.

Modern standardized intelligence tests are generally not considered technically biased against racial or ethnic groups because they show similar reliability and predictive validity across groups. While average group score differences have been observed, these differences do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the tests are biased. The reasons for those differences remain an active area of research and debate.


Myth 6: A Positive Attitude Can Stave off Cancer.

People with cancer often hear that they need to stay positive. But research hasn’t shown that keeping a positive attitude changes how long you live or how hard your experience with cancer will be.

Trying to be positive all the time can tire you out.  But studies also show that being optimistic when you have cancer can lead to a better quality of life. Many cancer survivors report that being optimistic makes their outlook on life better. Some also believe their disease, treatment outcomes, and survival do benefit from optimistic but realistic hopes. Find an approach that feels best for you.


Myth 7: Opposites Attract: We Are Most Romantically
Attracted to People Who Differ from Us.

The premise that we are most romantically attracted to people who differ from us is a myth; scientific studies show that humans are overwhelmingly drawn to partners who share similar traits, values, and backgrounds.

While small differences in hobbies or food choices can feel fun or exciting at first, major differences in core values often lead to long-term conflict.


Myth 8: Most Mentally Ill People Are Violent.

The belief that most people with mental illness are violent is a psychological myth. Research has consistently shown that the vast majority of individuals with mental health disorders are not violent and are more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators. Violent behavior is influenced by many factors, including substance abuse, past history of violence, and environmental conditions, rather than mental illness alone. This misconception contributes to stigma and discrimination, discouraging many people from seeking the help and treatment they need.

Other factors, such as drug or alcohol misuse and personal circumstances, play a much greater role. Spreading this myth increases fear and prejudice, making it more difficult for individuals with mental health conditions to receive understanding, support, and appropriate treatment.


Myth 9: Men and Women Communicate in Completely Different Ways.

The belief that men and women communicate in completely different ways is a psychological myth. Although some studies have found small differences in communication styles, these differences are often exaggerated. In reality, there is considerable overlap between how men and women express themselves, listen, and interact with others. Factors such as personality, culture, upbringing, education, and individual experiences have a much greater influence on communication than gender alone.

Research suggests that effective communication depends more on the individual than on whether they are male or female. Both men and women are capable of being empathetic listeners, confident speakers, and effective communicators in different situations.


Myth 10: Most People Who Were Sexually Abused in Childhood Develop Severe Personality.

The belief that most people who experience sexual abuse during childhood will develop severe personality problems is a psychological myth. Childhood sexual abuse is a serious and traumatic experience that can increase the risk of emotional and psychological difficulties. However, not everyone who has experienced such abuse develops severe personality problems. People's responses to trauma vary depending on factors such as resilience, family support, access to therapy, and other life experiences.

Research shows that many survivors are able to recover and lead healthy, fulfilling lives, especially when they receive appropriate support and treatment. While some individuals may develop conditions such as anxiety, depression, or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), severe personality disorders are not an inevitable outcome. <This message was edited>

11/09/2026, 5:11 pm - obstech systems: Guys, I want to say this once, clearly, and then I'm done — because I don't want this turning into an endless back-and-forth.

*What actually happened:*
A video was shared, and I tagged him on it as a joke — nothing more. We've done this kind of thing before, people got tagged, everyone laughed, nobody made it personal. There was zero intention to insult or target him specifically.

*What I got in return:*
Instead of a normal reaction — even a sarcastic one, or just telling me he didn't like it — I was abused directly, and my father was dragged into it with extremely vulgar language, in front of the entire group. That's not a proportionate response to a joke. That's a personal attack.

*Why I reacted the way I did:*
Let's be honest — this isn't a hypothetical. If someone insults you and your parents that badly, publicly, in front of people you see every day, staying silent isn't "maturity," it's just letting yourself be humiliated. I didn't start this exchange with abuse; I responded to abuse. There's a difference between provoking someone and defending yourself after being provoked.

I'll also be transparent: this isn't the first time. Something similar happened before in the PG, and I let it go without saying anything. I didn't escalate then. But a pattern that gets ignored once doesn't mean it should be tolerated indefinitely — especially when it repeats and gets worse.

*What I own:*
Yes, I used abusive language back. I'm not pretending otherwise, and I'm not going to dress it up as something else. But it was a reaction, not the opening move. If people are judging the reaction without weighing what triggered it, that's an incomplete picture of what happened — not a fair one.

*On bringing up past incidents:*
I'm aware there have been other situations involving him language and conflicts with people. I'm not listing them to win an argument or paint myself as the innocent one — I'm just saying context exists, and people are capable of forming their own judgment on that without me spelling it out.

*Where I stand now:*
I don't have personal hatred for anyone here, ..... We've got maybe a few months left before this four-year journey ends and everyone goes their own way — that's a strange thing to spend fighting over a group chat joke that went too far in both directions.

I've said my part, and I stand by it. If someone still feels my reaction was too harsh, that's a fair opinion to hold — but I'm not going to keep explaining or defending it over and over. As far as I'm concerned, this is closed on my end.
I also won't be replying in this thread after this. Anyone's free to share their point of view, that's fine — I just won't be part of the conversation going forward, except with him directly if needed.

No hate. 🤝❤️

The Aim of the test is to assess the level of academic achievement motivation of the subject using the Academic Achievement Motivation Test (AAMT) developed by Dr TR Sharma. 

The test was administered on ____

Table 1 shows the raw score, z score, and interpretation obtained by the subject. 

Academic Achievement Motivation refers to the internal drive, desire, and persistence that students show toward performing well in academic tasks, attaining educational goals, improving knowledge, and achieving academic success. It reflects how strongly a student values academic success and how much effort they are willing to invest to achieve it. In college, where students experience increased freedom, responsibility, and peer influence, motivation affects how they manage time, engage in coursework, respond to academic challenges, and balance academics with social life and lifestyle habits. Students with higher motivation tend to view education as a pathway to growth and opportunities, while those with lower motivation may struggle with procrastination, lack of academic identity, or difficulty linking academic effort to personal goals.

Students with high academic achievement motivation display strong goal orientation, self-discipline, and consistency in their study habits. They show curiosity, ask questions, actively participate in class, and seek clarification when needed. These students manage time effectively, maintain a regular study schedule, and respond constructively to feedback and academic challenges. They view difficulties as learning opportunities and show persistence, resilience, and a long-term focus on academic and career outcomes.

Students with moderate academic motivation work reasonably well but lack consistent effort across tasks or time. They study more when exams approach or when external pressure is present, and their performance depends on the interest level or perceived importance of the subject. They may engage in class and complete assignments, but not always proactively or deeply. Motivation fluctuates, leading to periods of productivity followed by procrastination, resulting in stable but not outstanding academic performance.

Students with low academic motivation often lack interest in academic tasks and have difficulty connecting coursework to personal goals. They may show irregular study habits, frequent procrastination, absenteeism, and minimal participation in class activities. These students tend to avoid academic challenges, feel easily discouraged by setbacks, and may rely on external circumstances rather than self-driven effort. Their lifestyle may prioritize leisure or social activities over academic responsibilities, leading to inconsistent or poor academic outcomes.

The subject obtained a total raw score of _, Z score of _, interpreted as _ level of academic achievement motivation. 

Factors Influencing Academic Achievement Motivation
Levels of academic achievement motivation are shaped by multiple interacting factors, including personal beliefs such as self-confidence and academic self-efficacy, interest in the subject, and emotional well-being. Family expectations, support, and home environment contribute to attitudes toward education, while the teaching style, classroom climate, and quality of feedback influence motivation at the institutional level. Peer groups and social norms can either encourage academic engagement or distract from it. Additionally, cultural values, career aspirations, financial circumstances, stress levels, and availability of study resources all play significant roles in determining how motivated a student feels toward academic achievement.


Improving Academic Achievement Motivation

Academic motivation can be improved by setting clear, realistic academic goals, developing structured study routines, and practicing time management. Students benefit from connecting academic tasks to personal interests and long-term career plans, which creates meaningful purpose behind effort. Positive self-talk, regular reflection on progress, and seeking help when needed enhance confidence and persistence. Teachers and institutions can support motivation by offering encouraging feedback, promoting interactive learning environments, and providing academic support systems such as mentoring and study groups. Building a balanced lifestyle that includes adequate sleep, physical activity, and emotional well-being also strengthens sustained academic motivation.

Conclusion
